title: Sustained air-breathing combined-cycle flight to orbital speed

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an orbital vehicle that uses oxygen collected from the atmosphere to burn its fuel through almost all of the energy gain needed to reach orbit. It would combine propulsion modes suited to different flight conditions, sustaining useful air-breathing thrust from takeoff or air launch through hypersonic ascent. A final rocket phase using stored oxidizer could complete orbital insertion after atmospheric oxygen becomes insufficient. The defining advance is the extent of the air-breathing ascent, rather than a particular engine layout.

Proposed scope: atmospheric oxygen would support propulsion until the vehicle had gained more than 90 percent of the mechanical specific-energy increase between its declared starting state and its target orbit. Horizontal takeoff and a single combined-cycle engine are possible implementations, but neither defines the broader capability. The supplied demonstrations and design descriptions establish relevant foundations; they do not demonstrate this proposed orbital capability.

significance.text: Obtaining oxygen from the atmosphere would avoid carrying the oxygen consumed during that portion of ascent. Extending this benefit through most of the required orbital energy gain would represent a major advance in orbital propulsion. NASA identifies greater payload capacity and reusable orbital launch vehicles among the motivations for scramjet research, although those potential benefits do not establish the performance of a vehicle meeting this proposal.

Engineering synthesis: a much higher payload fraction would remain conditional on the complete vehicle. Inlets, compressors or other propulsion hardware, cooling systems, structural reinforcement and thermal protection add mass; atmospheric flight also incurs drag and trajectory losses. These costs could offset some of the saved oxidizer mass. A convincing assessment would therefore compare delivered payload and total vehicle performance, rather than infer payload gains from oxygen collection alone.

A runway-capable implementation could support launch infrastructure based around airfields. SABRE's archived design explicitly included runway start and takeoff, showing how that architecture relates to air-breathing space access. However, runway operations are an architectural choice, and SABRE's intended transition to rocket mode near Mach 5 falls well short of the proposed air-breathing energy threshold.

Conditional downstream possibilities include more reusable launch operations, more frequent flights and potentially lower launch costs. These would require additional progress in maintenance, turnaround, infrastructure and operating economics. Airline-like fares, passenger certification and daily cadence would not follow from a propulsion demonstration alone. The airplane analogy is useful for an airfield-based architecture, but it does not establish comparable operating conditions or commercial reliability.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing integrated capability is sustained air-breathing propulsion across the ascent envelope and through nearly all of the required orbital energy gain, followed by successful orbital insertion. The supplied record documents short, rocket-boosted scramjet flights and a combined-cycle design intended to switch to rocket mode near Mach 5. It does not document the proposed full capability. These selected sources also cannot establish its absence from every program worldwide through 1 November 2026.

The technical challenge joins inlet operation, stable combustion and thermal survival over a wide range of speeds and atmospheric conditions. External vehicle speed must be distinguished from airflow inside the engine. A scramjet maintains supersonic flow through its combustor; a precooled compressor-based design slows the incoming air before compression and combustion. Consequently, success with one internal-flow arrangement does not establish that another arrangement can operate across the same flight envelope.

Engineering synthesis: an integrated vehicle must capture and process enough atmospheric oxygen as the air thins, maintain combustion and useful net thrust despite inlet and aerodynamic losses, and manage heating for the required duration. It must also transition between propulsion modes without losing vehicle control or exceeding thermal limits. Cooling, fuel delivery, structures and propulsion hardware must fit within a mass budget that still permits orbital insertion and useful payload. Separate component tests do not resolve these coupled vehicle-level requirements.

current_state.text: NASA's X-43A reached Mach 9.6 on 16 November 2004 after acceleration by a Pegasus booster. Its scramjet operated for about ten seconds, after which the vehicle glided into the Pacific without recovery. This demonstrated very high-speed atmospheric scramjet operation, rather than an ascent from takeoff to orbit. NASA's page, updated 15 August 2025, states that no scramjet flight test had surpassed that speed; this is the page's dated record statement, not a separately established worldwide finding for November 2026.

Boeing's X-51A flew on 1 May 2013 for about three and a half minutes on scramjet power and reached Mach 5.1. A solid-rocket booster first accelerated it to about Mach 4.8, and the flight ended with a dive into the Pacific. Boeing's release provides direct support for these figures in the supplied review. CNET corroborated the duration and peak speed in an article published on 3 May 2013, the same publication date as Boeing's release and two days after the flight. This longer powered flight still did not demonstrate orbital ascent or air-breathing operation from takeoff.

Reaction Engines' SABRE was an unfinished combined-cycle engine concept, rather than a flown orbital engine. Its company description, archived on 8 May 2022, presented intended air-breathing operation from rest to about Mach 5, with the intake closing beyond that range for rocket mode. The description also referred to roughly Mach 25 for space access in rocket mode. These were system design goals, not achieved flight speeds. The development account described separate precooler, core and thrust-chamber building blocks and ground component demonstrations; those results do not establish integrated orbital flight.

The supplied Wikipedia account gives more precise SABRE inlet-closure design figures of Mach 5.14 and 28.5 km altitude. These remain secondary figures because the underlying references were not supplied for inspection. They should not be treated as measured flight conditions or as verified limits for every precooled combined-cycle design.

FlightGlobal's article dated 1 November 2024 confirms that Reaction Engines had entered administration after failing to secure additional funding. The portion available to the supplied review was limited by a subscription barrier and did not expose the claimed appointment date of 31 October. The administration event is supported, while that exact date remains unverified in this record.

Coverage limitation: the supplied material contains no bounded freshness search establishing worldwide flight status as of 1 November 2026. Classified programs and potentially relevant non-English reports were not comprehensively reviewed. Unspecified reports of longer ground combustor runs cannot be assessed from this record and, even if confirmed, would establish ground endurance rather than orbital flight. These limitations leave the global present-day record open; they do not invalidate the documented X-43A or X-51A results.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: an uncrewed vehicle would take off, use atmospheric oxygen throughout its powered ascent before any stored-oxidizer operation, and enter a sustained target orbit. Stored oxidizer could first be used only after the vehicle had gained more than 90 percent of the mechanical specific-energy increase required between its declared takeoff state and that orbit. The 90 percent threshold is a proposal for this concept, not a published consensus requirement.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement definition: calculate mechanical specific energy in an Earth-centered inertial frame as kinetic plus gravitational potential energy per unit mass. Define the fraction gained as (energy at first stored-oxidizer use minus starting energy) divided by (target-orbit energy minus starting energy). This measures an energy increase and avoids ambiguity from the signed value of orbital specific energy. Declare the starting state, target orbit, calculation conventions and orbit-verification interval before flight. An air-launched variant would also need to disclose carrier assistance and its release-state energy so that the contribution of the air-breathing ascent remains clear.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed measurement definition

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidence package: provide independently assessable trajectory, propulsion-mode, fuel and oxidizer-flow records sufficient to establish the energy threshold and timing of stored-oxidizer use. Confirm orbital insertion and persistence over the declared verification interval. Document external assistance, payload, vehicle mass, operating conditions and thermal limits, so that a successful flight establishes a bounded capability rather than an ambiguous speed milestone.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed evidence package

completion_criteria.text: Proposed repeatability and practical boundaries: a second successful flight of the same vehicle class would demonstrate limited repeatability. Reflight of the same vehicle, if reuse is claimed, would supply additional evidence about durability and turnaround. Two flights would not establish operational reliability, passenger safety, favorable economics or performance across all trajectories and conditions. The demonstrated envelope should identify the payload, target orbit, launch conditions and allowable maintenance; broader claims would require further evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed repeatability and practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Architectural relationship: a single combined-cycle engine and horizontal takeoff are possible implementations of ROC-01. SABRE provides a documented example of a runway-oriented combined-cycle design, but its intended transition to rocket mode near Mach 5 addresses an earlier portion of ascent. The supplied material does not establish exact equivalence between ROC-01 and the referenced historical call for one engine and horizontal takeoff to orbit.

Roster-based synthesis: ROC-02, “Beamed-energy launch of a useful payload into orbit,” shares the objective of orbital access but obtains launch energy from an external beam. ROC-01 instead centers on obtaining atmospheric oxygen for onboard combustion. The two concepts change different parts of the launch system; possible hybrid implementations would not make their defining demonstrations equivalent.

Roster-based synthesis: ROC-03, “A directed-energy lightsail accelerated to a substantial fraction of light speed,” also involves externally supplied energy, but its defining objective is lightsail acceleration to a substantial fraction of light speed. That differs from ROC-01's atmospheric propulsion and orbital-insertion objective.

Roster-based synthesis: ROC-04, “Open-cycle gas-core nuclear rocket with high thrust and multi-thousand-second specific impulse,” and ROC-05, “Fission-fragment rocket with direct conversion of fragment momentum into thrust,” pursue advanced nuclear propulsion. They overlap with ROC-01 in seeking major propulsion gains, but their defining advances concern nuclear energy and momentum conversion rather than atmospheric oxygen collection. Each remains a separate concept.

Roster-based synthesis: ROC-06, “A plasma-magnet sail that takes useful delta-v from the solar wind,” also obtains a useful resource from its environment. Its proposed resource is solar-wind momentum in space, whereas ROC-01 obtains atmospheric oxygen to support combustion during ascent. Their environments, mechanisms and completion demonstrations differ.

Roster-based synthesis: ROC-07, “An operational momentum-exchange tether that moves payloads between orbits,” transfers momentum through an orbital tether system. The earlier candidate described a possible suborbital-airplane and tether-catch combination, but the supplied roster does not establish that specific architecture. Such a combination might share part of an atmospheric ascent with ROC-01, while relying on a different mechanism for subsequent energy transfer. ROC-07 should retain its independent identity.

Roster-based synthesis: ROC-08, “Industrial-scale production and loading of rocket propellant off Earth,” changes where propellant is produced and loaded. ROC-01 changes how oxygen is supplied during atmospheric ascent. They could contribute to the same transportation system, but off-Earth propellant production would not demonstrate ROC-01's air-breathing capability, and ROC-01 would not establish an off-Earth propellant industry.

change_log.change: Preserved ROC-01's identity while defining its central capability through atmospheric-oxygen propulsion across most of the required orbital energy gain.
change_log.reason: A single engine and horizontal takeoff are architectural options; the energy threshold expresses the broader proposed innovation.

change_log.change: Replaced the universal claim that no engine has achieved the capability with a bounded account of what the supplied evidence documents.
change_log.reason: The supplied review contains no comprehensive worldwide freshness search through 1 November 2026.

change_log.change: Distinguished external flight speed from internal engine airflow and limited the near-Mach-5 transition claim to SABRE.
change_log.reason: Scramjets retain supersonic combustor flow, while precooled compressor-based engines slow intake air; one design does not establish a universal architecture limit.

change_log.change: Retained the X-43A and X-51A speeds, durations, dates and booster dependence, and used Boeing's release as directly reviewed evidence.
change_log.reason: The validated review had access to the complete Boeing release, superseding the candidate's earlier statement that it had not been reloaded.
The flight occurred on 1 May 2013; Boeing's release and CNET's corroborating article were published on 3 May.

change_log.change: Separated SABRE design goals, secondary inlet-closure figures and ground component work from demonstrated integrated flight.
change_log.reason: Neither projected Mach ranges nor component demonstrations establish orbital air-breathing propulsion.

change_log.change: Qualified the exact Reaction Engines administration date and preserved the subscription-access limitation.
change_log.reason: The retained FlightGlobal excerpt supports administration by its 1 November 2024 publication date but does not expose the claimed 31 October appointment date.

change_log.change: Recast higher payload fraction, airfield infrastructure and airline-like operations as conditional outcomes.
change_log.reason: Oxidizer savings alone do not establish vehicle-level payload gains, a runway architecture or commercial operating performance.

change_log.change: Defined the proposed energy threshold relative to a declared starting state and target orbit in an Earth-centered inertial frame, and added bounded verification proposals.
change_log.reason: An energy increase avoids signed-orbital-energy ambiguity; explicit assistance, telemetry and operating boundaries make the proposed demonstration assessable.

change_log.change: Retained the two-flight proposal while limiting its interpretation to demonstrated repeatability.
change_log.reason: Two successful flights would not establish operational reliability or universal performance.

change_log.change: Explained relationships to every other supplied roster entry and qualified the earlier ROC-07 and historical-equivalence assertions.
change_log.reason: The roster supports broad conceptual distinctions but does not document a specific tether-catch launch architecture or the referenced historical call.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish the comprehensive worldwide flight record through 1 November 2026, including classified programs or potentially relevant non-English reporting.
SABRE's secondary inlet-closure figures of Mach 5.14 and 28.5 km have not been checked against their underlying design references.
The exact date of Reaction Engines' administration appointment remains unverified because the relevant FlightGlobal text was unavailable beyond the subscription barrier.
No complete vehicle analysis establishes payload fraction, net mass savings, thermal endurance, cost or practical operating cadence for the proposed greater-than-90-percent energy threshold.
A concrete demonstration would still need numerical choices for target orbit, verification interval, payload, measurement uncertainty and acceptable operating conditions.
An air-launched implementation requires an explicit accounting convention for carrier assistance and starting energy before its result can be compared fairly with takeoff-based demonstrations.
The referenced historical call and the candidate's specific suborbital-airplane/tether-catch description of ROC-07 are not documented in the supplied sources.
Unspecified longer ground combustor runs cannot be evaluated from the supplied material.
